meta.descrizione: A pixel-art action platformer, in development. Taranto, 2087: the arm comes with a subscription, revenge doesn’t. Play the demo in your browser.
meta.og_alt: The CTRL+ALT REVENGE! logo over GIG hitting a punk with the cyber arm in a Tamburi street red with dust, under the KEBAB · PANZEROTTI sign.

eroe.motto: Taranto, 2087. The arm comes with a subscription. Revenge doesn’t.
eroe.tocco: Play it on a computer: keyboard or gamepad.
eroe.video: Gameplay outside the kebab shop: jab, jab, cyber hook and kick on the punk, who finally goes down.

storia.nota: In the game, the story is told by Totò’s murals. These panels are illustrations made for the site with the game’s real art.

cartelloni.testo: White domes cover the old steelworks: beneath them, so they say, SIDERA’s great clean-up is under way, and by Easter the city will finally be pure.

Cataldo Gigante, GIG to everyone, is the engineer from the Tamburi district who designed MANODOPERA, the cybernetic arm that gave injured workers back the arm they had lost on the job, and which SIDERA now rents out by subscription.

After the death of Mimmo, his oldest friend, GIG asked too many questions: within a week he had lost his job, his home and his name on the patents, and his arm was locked remotely with two words: “Subscription expired.”
As the perdoni, hooded and barefoot, file out of the Carmine church, two Esattori, SIDERA’s repo men, track him down at Mimmo’s grave in San Brunone cemetery to repossess the arm.

GIG escapes to his mother’s garage, plugs his father’s old keyboard into the arm and hits <kbd>CTRL</kbd>+<kbd>ALT</kbd>+<kbd>CANC</kbd> (CANC is Delete on Italian keyboards), two keys with his one good hand and the third with his nose:

the arm reboots and starts to talk, his eye turns cyan, and with his first double jump his single night begins, that afternoon, on the rooftops of the Tamburi, where his guide is Totò, eleven years old, who sprays REVENGE on the walls.

storia.errore_label: The MANODOPERA window: subscription expired. Next to it, GIG’s portrait with his cyber eye switched off.
storia.tasti_aiuto: Press all three, like GIG: two with your good hand, the third with your nose.
storia.ritratto_spento: GIG, his cyber eye switched off.
storia.ritratto_acceso: GIG, his cyber eye switched on: it’s cyan.

mondo.sotto: Taranto, 2087: the world of the game
paragrafi: Since 2041 the old steelworks has been sealed under white domes marked “Construction site, no entry”. SIDERA calls it the clean-up, and has given it a name that sounds like a streaming service: ARIA+, “The air you deserve” (aria means air), with ARIA+ Alta Quota (“high altitude”) for those who can pay. A red cloud hangs over the city: the smoke, they say, is “clean-up steam”, the dust a “temporary inconvenience”. The Colombe (“doves”), white drones carrying the ARIA+ logo, measure the air and spray a fresh, clean scent; they are named after the wooden dove that tradition credits to Archytas, the engineer-philosopher of Greek Taranto. On the big screens, the Easter celebration is already being advertised: “Taranto is pure”.

The Tamburi is the working-class district pressed up against the steelworks: public housing blocks with small terraces, washing hung out to dry and turned red by the dust, windows stopped up with wet towels whenever the north-west wind blows the dust in. Everything that was once pale wears a red film, even the tombs of San Brunone cemetery. Above the streets runs the Linea (“the Line”): conveyor belts on concrete pylons that disappear under the domes. At the foot of the pylons stands Ignazio’s MiniBar, GIG’s local. Plenty of people here wear a MANODOPERA arm (the word means “workforce”, literally “the work of the hand”) with red rings, on a monthly subscription; miss a payment and the Esattori come knocking.

notte.testo: It all happens in a single night, from Holy Thursday into Good Friday, 17–18 April 2087, which is also the city’s oldest night.

orari.cosa: the perdoni, barefoot and hooded, leave the Carmine church and walk from church to church to pray at the Altars of Repose, with the slow, rocking step called the nazzicata;
from San Domenico in the Old Town, the procession of Our Lady of Sorrows (the Addolorata) sets out, led by the troccolante and his wooden clapper, the troccola.

notte.chiusa: By 2087 almost everything in Taranto has changed, except this.

esattori.nota: In the game there are four kinds of Esattori, all in dust goggles. Two are already in the demo’s prologue: the gig-economy rider, with an insulated delivery backpack, and the bailiff, who reads out the seizure order and calls for backup; still to come are the career collector, in a reflective ESATTORE vest, and the renter, with a rented arm. The punk and the brute shown above are the ones from chapter 2, and will become the rider and the career collector.

colombe.testo: White drones bearing the ARIA+ logo: they measure the air and spray a fresh, clean scent.
colombe.nota: They are already in the demo’s prologue, though their art is still a placeholder.

gioco.intro: A pixel-art action platformer, with combat arenas and hacking puzzles. This is the game we’re making: each pillar says what you can already try in the demo and what is still in development.

pilastri.titolo: Platforming and fights, in one night
pilastri.slice: in the prologue you run and jump, with the double jump once the arm reboots, and the camera tilts when the Esattori turn up; in chapter 2 there’s a live cable to jump and an arena fight that ends with ZONA LIBERATA (“zone cleared”).
pilastri.testo: You run and jump side-on in 2D, with a double jump from the moment the arm reboots, early in the prologue; when the Esattori turn up the camera tilts, the floor opens out and the fight moves into depth, like the side-scrolling arcade classics. When it’s over, VAI (“GO”) flashes up and you’re back to jumping.

pilastri.slice: jab, jab, cyber hook and kick; grabs with knee strikes and throws; the flying kick.
pilastri.sviluppo: a dodge into depth, a timed parry, the Scarica and things to throw.
pilastri.testo: The combo only continues if the blow connects: jab, jab, cyber hook, kick. Grabs with knee strikes and throws, where a thrown body bowls over anyone in the way, plus a flying kick. Coming next: a dodge into depth, a timed parry with the cyber arm that opens up a counter, the Scarica (an electric punch), and bins, pipes and crates to throw.

pilastri.slice: running, jumping, ledge grabs and slides; after the reboot, the Spinta.
pilastri.sviluppo: wall jumps, air dashes and wall runs, already in the test room, and the Rampino.
pilastri.testo: Run, variable-height jump and Spinta, a double jump kicked off by a downward blast from the arm; ledge grabs, slides, wall jumps, air dashes and wall runs. Later on, the Rampino, a grapple to swing from cables and chains like Pitfall’s vines. And the forgiving jump timing players expect today.

pilastri.sviluppo: the first hack, in the test room.
pilastri.testo: GIG plugs his arm into the SIDERA panels that his cyan eye, the Vista, reveals: he reverses the Linea’s belts, opens gates, reprograms the Colombe and switches off lasers. They’re timed hacking puzzles inside the level, Comix Zone style; the few biggest hacks get a full-screen mini-game, a data stream to route through a grid.

pilastri.slice: in the prologue, the first secrets and the first of Totò’s tags; after the reboot, the Vista and the first arm log.
pilastri.testo: The Vista cuts through the red dust of the Wind Days, when the north-west wind blows hard over Taranto, to reveal fake walls, invisible platforms and ARIA+ billboards that, looked at properly, point the way. Every act hides arm logs, secret-hunting in the Duke Nukem and Jazz Jackrabbit tradition: each tells a worker’s story, and the more you find, the richer the epilogue. On the walls, Totò’s tags to collect.
At certain moments you choose what GIG says. There’s no meter on screen, but the story remembers, right up to the ending.

pilastri.titolo: Taranto you can play, with today’s rules
pilastri.slice: San Brunone cemetery and the Tamburi; coffee, taralli and a panzerotto as pick-ups; the CONTINUA? screen, lives and checkpoints.
pilastri.testo: Real places, from San Brunone cemetery to the rooftops of the Tamburi, and the city’s own food as pick-ups: taralli, coffee from the MiniBar, panzerotti and the rare Easter scarcella, which pushes your health past the maximum. Three acts in a single night, a prologue and [[capitoli]] chapters, replayable for missed secrets; frequent checkpoints, unlimited retries and no GAME OVER, and for a thrill, an optional arcade mode with three lives and a CONTINUA? (“continue?”) screen.

demo.testo: The demo plays in your browser, with a keyboard or a gamepad. From the title screen, NUOVA PARTITA (“new game”) starts with the prologue (San Brunone cemetery, the escape through the Tamburi and the garage where the arm reboots, with mural cutscenes and voices) and carries on into chapter 2, “Il Wind Day”: GIG against the punk and the brute. CAPITOLI (“chapters”) lets you replay either one. All with the demo’s music.
demo.onesta: It’s a work-in-progress demo: the prologue isn’t finished (some distant backdrops and a few finishing touches are still missing), chapter 1 isn’t there yet, and the art, the text and the levels will change. The game’s own text and voices are in Italian, and in the browser all sounds come from the centre. The first load is the longest: the demo page says how much it downloads.

comandi.nota: With a gamepad, press any button so the browser picks it up. Try pressing the keys: they light up here.

tecnica.sotto: Pixel art is the style, not a period limitation.
paragrafi: The game runs at 480×270 pixels, scaled up by whole multiples, and uses modern techniques wherever they look better. The demo already has dynamic lights with normal maps on the characters, sparks and particles, hit-stop on impacts and slow motion on the final KO; the full game can also use a smooth camera, shaders and deformation.

The comic-book scenes, meaning the intro and the interludes, are Totò’s murals: pixel art in a street-art style, with spray-can gradients, drips, thick outlines and neon colours. The camera pans along the wall and the panels come alive with parallax, lights and particles. The prologue’s murals are done; those for the chapters, and the look of the sprites, may still change: everything here is work in progress.

This site follows the same rules: every pixel of the art is a game pixel, scaled up by a whole number of your screen’s pixels, and the cloud and the dust are drawn by the page’s own code, with old-school Bayer dithering.

luce.didascalia: GIG’s real sprite, with its normal map: move the pointer over the box, or use the arrow keys when it’s selected, and the light follows. Your browser computes it, the way Godot does in the game.
luce.label: GIG on guard, lit by a moving light: move it with the pointer or the arrow keys.

passi.testo: The characters start from free 3D models and animations released under CC0, by Quaternius and Mesh2Motion.
Blender animates and renders them. The key moves, meaning the grab, knee strikes, throw, cyber hook and flying kick, are poses written into the scripts.
Python scripts turn them into pixel art, with a palette for each material, stamps for facial details, a springy ponytail, procedurally built boots and a normal map for every sprite sheet.

The backgrounds start from painted bases made with ChatGPT and Gemini, from prompts written while looking at the real places of Taranto; our scripts turn them into the game’s pixel art. Chapter 2’s floor and cable are drawn by code, and the shop signs use our own pixel typeface. Fonts, effects and interface come from scripts too. The sound effects are built from ready-made, freely licensed sounds, trimmed and layered.
Godot puts it all together, with dynamic lights and fixed-tick logic.

catena.chiusa: The scripts, written by AI agents for Luigi Massari, are deterministic, use fixed seeds and are nearly all in the repository. AI-generated images are only ever bases: those of the settings, the murals and the title-screen backdrop, and the faces in the cutscene close-ups, made from our own 3D renders. In-game characters and enemies come from the 3D pipeline.

tappe.sotto: In development, November 2026. CTRL+ALT REVENGE is being rebuilt from scratch in Godot [[godot]], Windows first; the old Python/Pygame prototype is archived in the legacy-pygame branch.
tappe.prova: The score above is real: it comes from the demo replay the tests play back. With this version it always ends on tick [[tick]] with [[punteggio]] points and the same hash, [[hash]]…: the logic runs on fixed ticks and is deterministic, and the tests check it by playing the same replays twice. There are [[test]] groups of automated tests.

righe.testo: Written and approved from start to finish: prologue, three acts, ending and epilogue, with the comic-book intro and interludes.
Decided and written down: platforming and arenas, moves, combat, hacking puzzles, health and checkpoints, pick-ups, secrets, chapters and hazards.
Sourced research on Taranto, and a timeline that keeps places, dates, times, weather and even that night’s moon consistent.

It began as a technical slice and is now in the demo: GIG against the punk and the brute, with combos, grabs, knee strikes, throws, a flying kick, a live cable to jump and an arena that ends with ZONA LIBERATA. Version 7 sprites with normal maps and dynamic lights, synthesised sound effects (later replaced with ready-made sounds), and fixed-tick game logic checked by automated tests and deterministic replays.
Plain grey, to fine-tune the moves: jumps, double jump, ledges, slide, walls and dash, the switch to the arena with the tilting camera, the first Esattori and the first hack.

San Brunone cemetery, the escape through the Tamburi and the garage, with the arm’s reboot. Until the reboot, GIG fights with a dead arm. It’s already playable in the demo, with mural cutscenes and voices; still to do are some distant backdrops, a second pass on two stretches and the final sprite for one of the drones.
“The Rooftops of the Tamburi”, with Totò as GIG’s guide.
The murals for the chapters, and the soundtrack, with a ’90s sound but not necessarily chiptune.

tappe.slice: Chapter 2 began as a technical test. Since 7 November 2026 its street shows Taranto on the evening of Holy Thursday 2087, a Wind Day: the red cloud instead of a starry sky, wind and ore dust instead of rain, public housing blocks with reddened washing, the Linea’s tunnel, neighbourhood shop signs and the billboards of SIDERA and ARIA+.

crediti.ai: The images on this site are the game’s own art, made by deterministic scripts from the CC0 sources listed below and from the bases described further on, and what the page’s own code draws, like the cloud and the dust. The scripts are written by AI agents for Luigi Massari, and you can read nearly all of them in the repository: those for the prologue’s boards are still in our working folder. In the game, AI-generated images are only ever bases: the painted backgrounds and prop sheets of the prologue’s settings, made with Google’s Gemini app and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, the first ones from text-only prompts and, since 8 November 2026, also from our own bases and renders, never from anyone else’s images; the layers of chapter 2’s street, painted by ChatGPT over our own renders and sketches; the cutscene murals, including the one on the trailer’s poster, from ChatGPT bases, with the backgrounds from text-only prompts and the figures from our own 3D renders; the title-screen backdrop, from a ChatGPT base made from one of our own bases; and the faces in the cutscene close-ups, made with ChatGPT from our own 3D renders. The scripts turn them into pixel art and, in the game, animate the murals, the eyelids and the mouths. Only in the trailer are the murals animated with HeyGen. Gemini, ChatGPT, Suno and HeyGen are AI services, some on a paid subscription.

piede.finzione: CTRL+ALT REVENGE is a work of fiction, set in a Taranto of 2087 imagined from the real city. SIDERA, ARIA+, MANODOPERA and all the characters are invented. Any resemblance to real people or companies is coincidental. The city’s places and rituals are real, and we portray them with respect.

contesto.testo: The story was written in November 2026, in the days when Taranto’s blast furnaces began to be shut down. The game doesn’t retell the news: it imagines Taranto sixty years on, and takes aim at those in power, never at the people who live there, work there or have fallen ill.
